numberItems.stem: At speeds below 40 mph, what following-distance rule does the handbook give?
options: 1 second for each 10 feet of vehicle length
1 second for each 10 feet of vehicle length, plus 1 more second
4 seconds, whatever the vehicle length
numberItems.explanation: Below 40 mph you need at least 1 second for each 10 feet of vehicle length; above 40 mph add 1 second (p. 2-19).

numberItems.stem: How does the following-distance rule change above 40 mph?
options: Add 1 second for every 10 mph over 40
Use the same rule, then add 1 second
Double the time
numberItems.explanation: Above 40 mph, use the same formula (1 second per 10 feet) and add 1 second, once (p. 2-19).

numberItems.stem: You drive a 40-foot truck at 65 mph. What following distance do you need?
options: 4 seconds
6 seconds
5 seconds
numberItems.explanation: A 40-foot vehicle needs 4 seconds below 40 mph and 5 seconds above 40 mph; you add 1 second only once (p. 2-19).

numberItems.stem: You drive a 60-foot rig at 30 mph. How many seconds of following distance do you need?
options: 6 seconds
7 seconds
3 seconds
numberItems.explanation: At speeds below 40 mph a 60-foot rig needs 6 seconds (1 second per 10 feet); above 40 mph it needs 7 (p. 2-19).

numberItems.stem: You drive a 50-foot truck at 55 mph. How many seconds of following distance do you need?
options: 5 seconds
6 seconds
7 seconds
numberItems.explanation: 50 feet = 5 seconds, plus 1 second above 40 mph = 6 seconds (Figure 2.12, p. 2-19).

numberItems.stem: You drive a 30-foot vehicle at 55 mph. How many seconds of following distance do you need?
options: 3 seconds
5 seconds
4 seconds
numberItems.explanation: 30 feet = 3 seconds, plus 1 second because you are above 40 mph = 4 seconds (p. 2-19).

numberItems.stem: How do you measure your following distance?
options: Wait until the vehicle ahead passes a fixed landmark, then count "one thousand-and-one, one thousand-and-two…" until you reach it
Estimate the number of car lengths between you
Check that you can see the rear tires of the vehicle ahead
numberItems.explanation: Wait until the vehicle ahead passes a shadow, pavement marking or other landmark, then count off the seconds until you reach the same spot (p. 2-19).

numberItems.stem: What are the 2 dangers of traveling alongside other vehicles?
options: Wind blast, and road spray from the other vehicle
Another driver may change lanes suddenly into you, and you may be trapped when you need to change lanes
The other driver may flash lights at you, and your mirrors may touch
numberItems.explanation: There are 2 dangers in traveling alongside others: another driver may change lanes suddenly and turn into you, and you may be trapped when you need to change lanes (p. 2-20).

numberItems.stem: Why shouldn't you trust the height posted on a bridge or overpass?
options: Heights are posted with a safety margin of several feet
Posted heights apply only to empty vehicles
Repaving or packed snow may have reduced the clearance since it was posted
numberItems.explanation: Do not assume posted heights are correct; repaving or packed snow may have reduced clearance (p. 2-20).

numberItems.stem: How does the load in a cargo van affect its height?
options: A loaded van sits higher than an empty one
An empty van is higher than a loaded one
The load does not change the van's height
numberItems.explanation: An empty van is higher than a loaded one, so clearing a bridge loaded doesn't mean you will clear it empty (p. 2-20).

numberItems.stem: Your truck cannot make a tight right turn without swinging wide. What is the correct ("button hook") method?
options: Swing wide to the left first, then turn right
Turn wide as you complete the turn, keeping the rear of the vehicle close to the curb
Start the turn from the left lane
numberItems.explanation: Turn wide as you complete the turn (button hook), keeping the rear close to the curb; swinging left first (jug handle) is incorrect (p. 2-20).

numberItems.stem: You are turning right and a car is coming toward you in the lane you must cross into. What should you do?
options: Give the car room to pass, or stop — do not back up
Back up so the car has more room
Speed up to finish the turn first
numberItems.explanation: If you must cross into the oncoming lane, watch for traffic; give it room or stop, but do not back up (p. 2-20).

numberItems.stem: Where should you begin a left turn?
options: As soon as your front wheels cross the stop line
Before entering the intersection, to allow for off-tracking
After you reach the center of the intersection
numberItems.explanation: On a left turn, make sure you have reached the center of the intersection before you start the turn; turning too soon lets off-tracking hit a vehicle (p. 2-20).

numberItems.stem: An intersection has 2 left-turn lanes. Which one should you use?
options: The right-hand lane
The left-hand (inside) lane
Whichever lane is empty
numberItems.explanation: If there are 2 turning lanes, always take the right turn lane (p. 2-21).
